The distinguishing factors are that it's decentralized, open to anyone, and can't be co-opted by any government or corporation. It's the first time in history we had this capability. That's a big deal.

Predictable (and eventually fixed) supply. This is a critically important feature of 'sound money.' 'Sound money' is something a truly free market requires in order to actually work. Bitcoin has the potential (if it doesn't fail) to be 'sound money' someday.

Not only would bitcoin provide a stable supply of money (like a yardstick that doesn't change length on the vagaries of the political winds,) but it can provide an un-censorable method for individuals anywhere in the world to exchange value with one another. No interference from a local warlord (elected or not.) If Bitcoin succeeds, for the first time in history, the world will have the ability to revel in the freedom to voluntarily trade what you have for what you want.
The only reason Bitcoins are valuable is because people are willing to give you things in return for them. So if interest in BTC decreases, it could lose value as well.

This may be true for some people, but its not at all true in all cases. Bitcoin can be used as a token to represent digital assets on an immutable ledger -- used to write transactions (and input permanent data of your choosing) on the block chain. I could for instance write a song, put it on the blockchain, and would forever have proof that I control that data so long as I had the private key. I would control the earliest provable instance of that song, and it will one day represent a powerful type of evidence for settling disputes about data ownership. It's called cryptographic proof of existence, and people will buy bitcoin to use it for that purpose and other very powerful but related purposes.

Imagine the government is accused of altering a document, and committing a serious fraud against its own people. How would someone prove the document had been altered? Well, if all government documents are hashed and the hash is placed in a bitcoin transaction, those hash values will serve as a fingerprint. Only documents which had not been altered will produce the correct hash. Otherwise you can prove, definitively, that it is not the same document. Proof! and until we had an immutable ledger this was impossible. These functions give digital currencies intrinsic value.

The blockchain is the first time in history that we have triple entry accounting: credit, debit, and timestamp. Its the first time in history we can use the absence of presence as proof of absence: if the transaction is not in the database, it didn't happen.
